stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p > 0.05", Sentence = "Considering the 95% credible interval for the ACME crosses zero, the mediation effect is not significant at p > 0.05."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. Speech perception is a complex process involving integrating auditory and visual information.
In face-to-face interactions, people leverage auditory speech and visual cues, known as audiovisual (AV) speech, to understand spoken language.
This cross-modal enhancement relies on temporal and phonetic cues (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Munhall et al., 2004).

text.text: Studies with native English speakers show that sensitivity to visual temporal cues (i.e., opening of the mouth that indicates onset of speech) emerges in infancy (around four months) and becomes highly developed by six months (e.g., Grant, van Wassenhove & Poeppel, 2004; Lalonde & Werner, 2019; Lewkowicz, 2000 Lewkowicz, , 2010)).

text.text: Sensitivity to visual phonetic cues (i.e., mouth movements that correspond to specific speech sounds, termed audiovisual [AV] cues) appears to mature more slowly, typically reaching full development around ages 6 to 9 in monolingual speakers of languages such as English (Lalonde & Holt, 2016), Dutch (Baart et al., 2014; 2015), and French-Canadian (Tremblay et al., 2007).

text.text: The 6-9-year age range is not arbitrary; it coincides precisely with the onset of reading instruction, a pivotal phase characterized by the transformative power of reading on phonological awareness (PA), an ability to recognize, discriminate, and manipulate sounds of a language (Anthony & Francis, 2005; Jerger et al., 2009).

text.text: As children engage with written text, they move beyond mere auditory decoding.
Their sensitivity to visual speech cues, linking lip and articulatory movements to phonemic representations, begins to increase.
For example, knowing that the word 'bat' starts with a bilabial closure of the mouth that corresponds to the /b/ sound indicates that a child has phonemic awareness of the sound /b/.

As a result, PA, which relies heavily on both the speaker's (Carrol et al., 2003; Johnson & Goswami, 2010) and the listener's LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION mouth articulation movements (Jerger et al., 2009), develops into a sophisticated cognitive resource vital for proficient reading (Gillon, 2017).
text.formatted: As a result, PA, which relies heavily on both the speaker's <ref type="bibr">(Carrol et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Johnson & Goswami, 2010</ref>) and the listener's LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION mouth articulation movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Jerger et al., 2009)</ref>, develops into a sophisticated cognitive resource vital for proficient reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gillon, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This dual-channel AV processing not only enhances children's PA but also augments their ability to decode written language (Carrol et al., 2003; Johnson & Goswami, 2010).
text.formatted: This dual-channel AV processing not only enhances children's PA but also augments their ability to decode written language <ref type="bibr">(Carrol et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Johnson & Goswami, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, the possible convergence of reading acquisition and increased sensitivity to AV speech cues remains understudied, despite the developmental overlap in the emergence of these skills.
Although interest in the development of AV speech perception has grown, relatively little research has examined its relation with children's PA and reading skills.

Decades of research has demonstrated that PA in children is strongly associated with their reading skills (e.g., Deacon & Kirby, 2004; McBride-Chang et al., 2005; Torgesen et al., 1997), as well as with their sensitivity to visual speech cues (e.g., Heikkilä et al., 2017; Norrix et al., 2007).

text.text: Some phonemes might be hard to distinguish by access to auditory signals alone but are relatively easy to distinguish by having access to complementary visual information (e.g., /n/ and /m/; Campbell, 2008).

text.text: Thus, the information conveyed by visual speech perception is incorporated into phonological representations and facilitates the development of PA.

In support of this claim, studies with deaf populations show that deaf individuals who use cued speech, a system that uses mouth articulations of speech (i.e., visual speech) in combination with hand gestures (Cornett, 1967), have better English PA skills than deaf individuals who do not use cued speech in combination with hand gestures (Colin et al., 2007: language = English).

text.text: Furthermore, some studies suggest that deficits in AV speech perception may relate to impaired PA skills.

These studies report that visual information has less influence on speech perception in individuals with phonological processing impairment (Meronen et al., 2013: language = Finnish; LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION Norrix et al., 2007: language = English).

text.text: The authors reported that only 14% of children with language impairment correctly identified incongruent AV speech (visual [bi] paired with auditory [gi]), compared with 54% of children with no language impairment.

text.text: This evidence suggests a relationship between PA and AV speech perception skills.
The onset of reading instruction may strengthen the link between PA and AV speech sensitivity by increasing the demand to integrate auditory and visual cues.
Reading entails establishing connections between phonemes (auditory/articulatory representations of sounds) and graphemes (visual representations) (Ehri, 2005; Ziegler & Goswami, 2005).
text.formatted: Reading entails establishing connections between phonemes (auditory/articulatory representations of sounds) and graphemes (visual representations) <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Ehri, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Ziegler & Goswami, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: To successfully establish these associations when reading, children need to accomplish several tasks.
They must first be able to auditorily identify phonemes while accounting for allophonic variations (i.e., natural variations in a phoneme's pronunciation).
They must then learn to visually recognize and differentiate graphemes, and map target phonemes with their corresponding grapheme (Horlyk et al., 2012).
text.formatted: They must then learn to visually recognize and differentiate graphemes, and map target phonemes with their corresponding grapheme <ref type="bibr">(Horlyk et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the ability to detect and match phonemes to graphemes involves both auditory and visual codes, which play a crucial role in deciphering spoken and written language.

Given that the integration of graphemes and speech sounds develops during reading acquisition, it is reasonable to expect a bidirectional relationship between reading skill and the developmental shift in sensitivity to AV speech cues in speech perception.

In fact, in a study examining the association between reading skills and phonemic discrimination (discriminating between native [English] speech sounds and non-native [Hindi] speech sounds), Burnham (2003) LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION found that 6-and 8-year-old children with higher reading scores showed higher phonemic discrimination scores for native contrasts versus non-native contrasts.

Languages exhibit a spectrum of orthographic depth, ranging from high opacity to high transparency: in orthographically "opaque" languages, the degree of phoneme-grapheme correspondence is very low (e.g., English, non-diactritical Hebrew); in orthographically "transparent" languages, there is a one-to-one correspondence between graphemes and phonemes (e.g., Turkish, German) (Katz & Frost, 1992).

text.text: The only studies to examine the relationship between AV speech perception and reading skills in typically developing school-aged children used English-speaking children tested with English (opaque orthography) language stimuli.

These studies found that increased sensitivity to language-specific phonetic cues (i.e., PA) mediated the relationship between AV speech sensitivity and reading ability (e.g., Erdener & Burnham, 2013).

text.text: However, the relationship between multimodal speech perception and reading skills in languages with transparent orthography remains uncharted territory.
To this goal, this study examines the relationship between sensitivity to AV speech perception cues and reading skills (reading and PA) in children who speak Uzbek.
Uzbek is one of the less-studied languages in language acquisition and reading development.
Unlike widely researched languages on AV speech perception and reading (e.g., English, Dutch), Uzbek has a transparent orthography.
This feature offers an opportunity to investigate how children acquiring reading skills in a language with orthographic transparency use AV cues during reading.

In this study, we examined whether learning to read affects sensitivity to visual phonological cues in speech perception and whether PA skills mediate the relationship between reading and AV speech perception.

Specifically, we examined children in grades 1 to 4 who were learning to read in a transparent language, Uzbek, and kindergarten children who had not yet started formal reading instruction (ages 5-6 years).

As children begin their reading journey and learn to associate visual representations of phonemes with their spoken counterparts, their LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION sensitivity to AV cues may increase as their reading skills improve.
Based on this central hypothesis, we predicted the following:
Readers' experience developing connections between speech sounds and their corresponding written representations may enhance their ability to integrate AV information during language processing.

Moreover, more skilled readers, compared with less skilled readers, have developed more robust links between written and spoken language, allowing them to integrate visual and auditory information more effectively during reading and speech perception tasks.

Therefore, we predicted that (1) readers (i.e., children in grades 1-4) would show greater sensitivity to AV cues compared to non-readers (i.e., kindergarteners), and (2) more proficient readers would also show greater sensitivity to AV cues, while less proficient readers would show weaker sensitivity to AV cues. .

Furthermore, adding a group variable (monolingual vs. bilingual) in the analyses of the current study did not affect the reported results and no significant effects of the group variable were observed, neither as a main effect nor in interaction with other variables (see Supplementary Materials for the results with the group variable).
Therefore, we report results collapsing across groups.

text.text: The assessment of children's PA skills in Uzbek included untimed tasks of initial sound identification, initial sound discrimination from the Early Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA; Gove & Wetterberg, 2011; RTI International, 2009), and phoneme segmentation from the Yopp-Singer segmentation task (Yopp, 1995).

text.text: The initial sound identification task was exclusively administered to younger children (age 5-6 years).
During this task, children were presented with 10 monosyllabic and bisyllabic words in Uzbek, such as "bo'sh" or "sho'x."
Their objective was to recognize and verbally express the first sound of each word, such as b for "bo'sh" or sh for "sho'x."
The initial sound discrimination task was given to school-aged children (grades 1-4).
In this task, the children listened to sets of three words and identified which word initiated with a different sound than the others in the set.
This task involved 10 sets of three words each; in each set, two words began with the same sound, and the initial sound for the third word was different, such as "bo'sh", "sho'x", "bor".
The position of the "different" word in the set varied.
The experimenter read each group of three words aloud slowly, two times, and asked the child to choose the word that begins with a different sound.
The phoneme segmentation task was administered to all children.
During this task, children listened to a list of 10 monosyllabic CVC or bisyllabic CVCVC words one by one.
Subsequently, they were required to recognize and articulate each sound within the word.

Children's reading proficiency in Uzbek was assessed using timed letter, non-word and passage reading tasks from the Early Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) previously used in Uzbekistan (Harden et al., 2022, RTI International).

text.text: Reading tasks were tailored for each grade level, with separate versions for grades 1-2 and grades 3-4, ensuring appropriateness and alignment with the respective curriculum levels.

Grade 1 participants engaged in letter and non-word reading tasks, wherein they were asked to read 100 Uzbek graphemes (e.g., "b", "v") and 50 non-words conforming to the orthographic structure of Uzbek (e.g., "incha").
The allotted time for these tasks was 60 seconds each, with a practice item preceding each task.
For grades 2, 3, and 4, the tasks were focused on non-word reading and passage reading.
Similarly, they were presented with 50 non-words for the non-word reading task, and the time limit remained at 60 seconds.
The passage reading task was adjusted based on the grade level.
Children in grade 2 were given 180 seconds to read the text aloud, while those in grades 3 and 4 were allotted only 60 seconds.
The goal was to assess reading fluency at a developmentally appropriate level for each grade.

This approach ensured that the assessment was tailored to children's cognitive abilities and reading skills in each grade, making it a comprehensive and developmentally sensitive evaluation of their reading proficiency.

These specific syllables were chosen as these syllables are found, and the differences between these consonants are highly salient in Uzbek.
To ensure natural spoken language representation and eliminate bias, each syllable was recorded in four versions, all of which were included in the experimental setup.
The video files were cropped to display only the speaker's face from the shoulders up against a white background.
The audio component of each video file was converted into uncompressed waveform audio files (wav) to serve as auditory stimuli.
These auditory stimuli had a resolution of 24 bits and a sampling rate of 48 kHz.
Each stimulus had a fixed duration of 2 seconds, which included the pre-and post-phonatory visual movements in addition to the acoustic syllabic signal.
On average, the acoustic signal associated with each syllable lasted approximately 0.43 seconds (range=0.3-0.6).

This variation in syllable duration accounted for the silent pre-and post-phonatory visual movements, which averaged 0.9 seconds before the onset of the acoustic signal (range=0.9-0.1) and 0.57 seconds after the offset of the acoustic signal (range=0.3-0.6).
This design facilitated the replication of natural prosodic characteristics of spoken language, providing a more ecologically valid representation of natural speech.

To ensure precise alignment and synchronization of the auditory and visual components of the stimuli, software tools such as iMovie (Version 10.3.5; macOS 13.0.1) and Audacity (Version 3.0.2) were employed.
Each stimulus began with a closed mouth followed by silent prephonatory mouth movements preceding the onset of the acoustic signal.
These prephonatory movements were used to simulate the anticipatory mouth gestures typically observed before the articulation of speech sounds.
The inclusion of this brief visual precursor aimed to enhance the naturalness and ecological validity of the audiovisual stimuli.
Testing was completed in a quiet room.
The AV speech perception task was administered via Pyschopy (v2021.2.3) using a 13-inch MacBook Pro (2.3 GHz Dual-Core Intel Core i5, macOS 13.0.1) and professional monitor headphones (ATH M20x).
The reading and PA tasks were administered using physical copies of each task.
For the AV speech portion task, participants were presented with non-target, target, and foil trials.

Participants were told that they would hear a stream of syllables (non-target and foil trials) and were instructed to press any key on a computer keyboard upon hearing a different syllable (target trials).
Target (N=10) and foil (N=10) trials were randomly mixed with the continuous presentation of the non-target syllable /ba/, occurring at a rate of one every 3 seconds in each experimental condition.
During non-target trials, there were no changes in the auditory and visual signals from the background syllable.
Target trials featured the syllable /da/, whereas, in foil trials, the visual cue suggested the target trial, but the auditory signal continued to be the background trial signal.
The inclusion of foil trials aimed to ensure that participants responded to AV signals rather than just visual cues (Lalonde & Werner, 2019).
text.formatted: The inclusion of foil trials aimed to ensure that participants responded to AV signals rather than just visual cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lalonde & Werner, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To habituate participants with non-target trials, 83% of the trials were non-target and foil (50 trials), while 17% were target trials (10 trials).
The sequencing of the trials was randomized, with no more than two identical trials occurring in succession.
Each stimulus had a duration of 2000 milliseconds with an LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION inter-stimulus interval (ISI) of 1000 milliseconds.
A 15-second break was provided between conditions.
To eliminate bias, the experimenter remained seated across from the participant, behind the computer screen throughout the experiment, and prompted participants to focus on the screen when needed.
Furthermore, children wore headphones to ensure that the experimenter could not hear the syllables being presented.
The entire procedure of the AV speech perception task lasted approximately 10 minutes per child.
For the PA and reading tasks, the experimenter first explained the task requirements to each child.
Following the introduction of the task requirements, each child was given a practice item to ensure their complete understanding of the task.
To avoid potential order effects, the sequence of testing for the AV speech perception, PA, and reading tasks was counterbalanced across participants.
This counterbalancing ensured that the order of task presentation did not systematically favor one task over the other, minimizing any potential biases introduced by the testing order.

text.text: Several data transformations and processing steps were undertaken to prepare the data for further statistical analyses.
The PA task scores were averaged to create a composite PA score.
Due to the non-normal distribution of PA composite scores, a rank transformation was applied to normalize the data between 0 and 1.
Rank transformation helps meet the normality of residuals assumption by LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION mapping the data to a uniform distribution.
This transformation served the dual purpose of normalizing the distribution and mitigating the impact of potential outliers.
As reading tasks had different scoring scales, the reading scores were standardized across all grades.
This ensured that all scores were on the same scale for comparison.
This approach enabled the comparison of reading performance and the creation of composite scores that combined data from multiple reading-related tasks.

Composite scores for reading were calculated by combining standardized scores as follows: for grades 2, 3, and 4, the composite score was the average of the z-scores for Nonword and Passage reading; for grade 1, the composite score was the average of the z-scores for Letter Reading and Nonword Reading.
These composite scores provided an overall measure of reading ability.
In the next step, outliers were identified and removed from composite scores using the interquartile range method, resulting in the removal of 2 observations.

Participants' ability to discriminate between target and non-target syllables in the AV speech perception task was calculated using the sensitivity index d' based on the signal detection theory (Green & Swets, 1966).

The raw d' scores were censored at about +4, resulting in a non-normal distribution.
We conducted three models to examine our predictions.
Our models included d' scores for AV cues as the outcome variable, while group (pre-readers, readers), and reading composite scores were included as main predictors; PA was included as a mediator.
Our first model was designed to investigate the main effects of group (pre-readers, readers) on d' scores for AV cues.
Our second model was designed to investigate the main effects of reading skill on AV stimuli d' scores for AV cues.
Our third model was designed to investigate the mediating effect of PA on the relationship between reading skills and sensitivity to AV cues.
Since the non-word reading was the task that was completed by all the grades, we also conducted our second and third models with non-word reading scores as a measure of reading proficiency.
The results of the models with non-word reading scores as a predictor did not show significant deviation from our results with reading composite scores as a predictor.
Results of the models with non-word reading scores are included in the Supplementary Materials.
In our first two models, to address censoring in our estimation, we fitted Bayesian linear models with an upper limit for d' scores for AV cues set at +4.
We utilized the brm function in the "brms" package developed by Bürkner (2017) to implement the models.

The Gaussian family was specified for the likelihood function.
Four sampling chains ran for 2000 iterations with a warm-up period of 1000, resulting in 4000 post-warm-up samples.
We used the default priors of the brms package.
In our third model, we initially performed two linear regression analyses utilizing the lm function within R (R Core Team, 2023).
The first model aimed to predict PA based on reading skills, while the second model aimed to predict sensitivity to AV cues based on both PA and reading.

Subsequently, these two models were integrated into a mediation model using the LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION mediate function from the "mediation" package developed by Tingley et al. (2013).

Confidence intervals were estimated at 95%, employing 3000 simulations to derive robust estimates of the mediation effect and associated intervals.

text.text: Our study explored the relationship between sensitivity to AV cues for speech perception, reading skills, and PA in Uzbek-speaking children aged 4 to 10 years.

Our findings shed light on the intricate interplay between reading development and sensitivity to AV cues, particularly in the context of learning to read in Uzbek, a language with a transparent orthography.

Broadly, our results showcase a relationship between reading skills and sensitivity to AV cues, with more LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION skilled readers displaying increased sensitivity to AV cues.
However, our results show no mediation effect of PA in the relationship between reading and sensitivity to AV cues for Uzbek.

In a simple way of testing whether the onset of exposure to reading instruction was associated with increased AV speech sensitivity, we compared groups of pre-readers (i.e., 5-6-year olds) and readers (i.e., 7-to 10-year olds).
Contrary to our predictions, we did not find effects of pre-reader vs reader group on AV speech sensitivity.
This might be due to potential influences of exposure to print materials and reading-related activities prior to formal schooling.
Children in our study population likely had some degree of reading exposure through activities such as being read to at home or in pre-school, exposure to nursery rhymes, and language games.
Previous research suggests that such early reading exposure contributes to the enhancement of vocabulary and PA, which are associated with increased sensitivity to AV cues (Jerger et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Previous research suggests that such early reading exposure contributes to the enhancement of vocabulary and PA, which are associated with increased sensitivity to AV cues <ref type="bibr">(Jerger et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it is plausible that the lack of significant difference in AV sensitivity observed in readers vs pre-readers could be attributed, in part, to both groups receiving some reading exposure, be it at home or at school.
However, the specific nature and extent of this preschool reading exposure were not assessed in our study, representing a limitation.

Future research could benefit from exploring the role of preschool reading exposure and the home reading environment in shaping speech perception abilities and its interaction with formal reading training in school.
Moreover, it is important to note that the onset of reading instruction was confounded with age, and older children generally demonstrated better AV speech sensitivity compared to younger children.

Isolating the effects of formal reading instruction on AV speech sensitivity (i.e., beyond the impacts of age) would require longitudinal research tracking individuals throughout pre-reading and reading stages to provide deeper insights into the developmental LITERACY AND AUDIOVISUAL SPEECH PERCEPTION trajectories of AV speech perception in readers vs pre-readers.

Outside of contexts where children have limited access to written materials prior to starting school and the age at which children enroll in school is highly variable (i.e., low-resource contexts in the Majority World; Whitehead et al., 2024; Jasińska et al., 2023), comparisons of pre-readers and readers have an age confound.
Hence, examining variation in reading skill in relation to AV speech perception is key.

Although exposure to reading instruction (i.e., being a reader relative to a non-reader) was not itself associated with greater AV speech sensitivity, stronger reading skills were associated with increased AV speech sensitivity.
This suggests that higher reading proficiency is associated with an overall enhanced ability to perceive and integrate auditory and visual information.
Importantly, even after accounting for the effect of age, reading skill was still a significant predictor of speech perception.
This indicates that while age-related factors predict speech perception, reading skill still explains additional variance in speech perception beyond age (Sekiyama & Burnham, 2008).

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether higher reading skills lead to improved speech perception or if children with better speech perception tend to develop higher reading skills.
The directionality of the relationship between AV speech sensitivity and reading skills necessitates further investigation assuming a longitudinal design.

To investigate whether greater sensitivity to AV speech in stronger readers was related to stronger phonetic and visual integration (i.e., in PA), we explored the mediation effect of PA in the relationship between reading and sensitivity to AV cues.

Even when controlling for mediating effects of PA, we found a significant total and direct effect of reading on sensitivity to AV cues, underlining the connection between reading proficiency and perceptual sensitivity, as observed in

However, PA did not significantly mediate the relationship between reading skill and AV speech sensitivity in Uzbek.

This lack of a mediation holds significance when viewed through the lens of literature emphasizing the transformative impact of reading acquisition on phonological representations (Harm and Seidenberg, 1999, 2004; Jasińska et al., 2024; Muneaux and Ziegler, 2004; Taft and Hambly, 1985; Taft, 2006).

text.text: Prior studies have consistently shown that learning to read influences phonological representations; literate individuals demonstrate superior performance in phonological tasks compared to non-literate counterparts (Castro-Caldas et al., 1998; Reis & Castro-Caldas, 1997), indicating the enhancement of PA skills driven by reading exposure.

text.text: This integration reflects the brain's adeptness at processing orthographic as well as auditory input.

In languages with opaque orthography, the multiple spelling variations for words with similar sounds result in less regular mapping, prompting increased cognitive effort to reconcile phoneme to grapheme inconsistencies, likely leading to prolonged reaction times for speech perception (Harm and Seidenberg, 1999; 2004; Pattamadilok et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In languages with opaque orthography, the multiple spelling variations for words with similar sounds result in less regular mapping, prompting increased cognitive effort to reconcile phoneme to grapheme inconsistencies, likely leading to prolonged reaction times for speech perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Harm and Seidenberg, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pattamadilok et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, in opaque orthographic languages, the incongruity between spelling and pronunciation might necessitate reliance on multiple information sources, such as visual speech cues to a greater extent than the auditory-only speech cues, to comprehend spoken language effectively, at least in the contexts when visual speech cues are relevant.

This echoes findings from languages with opaque orthography (Lalonde & Werner, 2021 for review), where children showed increased sensitivity to AV cues at the period that corresponds to the onset of reading instruction (age=6-9 years).
text.formatted: This echoes findings from languages with opaque orthography <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Lalonde & Werner, 2021</ref> for review), where children showed increased sensitivity to AV cues at the period that corresponds to the onset of reading instruction (age=6-9 years).

text.text: Our current findings, with a transparent orthography, such as Uzbek, suggest that challenges related to phoneme-grapheme correspondences could, to some extent (i.e., ~33%), contribute to differential sensitivity to AV speech cues at the onset of reading instruction.

The direct and reliable mapping between orthography and phonology in a language like Uzbek might enable readers to effortlessly associate visual symbols with their corresponding auditory representations; i.e., without having to sort through multiple visual-to-auditory correspondences in multi-modal cue integration.
This streamlined cognitive process is conducive to efficient decoding and comprehension of written and spoken language.
As children learning to read in transparent orthographies progress in reading proficiency, their increased PA likely contributes to a heightened sensitivity to AV cues.
It is imperative to recognize that speech development during childhood is a nuanced process that does not universally prioritize a singular modality over another.
This foundational acknowledgment underscores the complexity inherent in understanding the developmental trajectory of speech perception in early life.

While our study highlights the link between reading and AV speech perception, it is crucial to recognize that these findings might not fully capture the diversity of linguistic experiences across different languages.
The link between reading acquisition and AV speech perception could vary significantly depending on linguistic characteristics such as phonological structure and orthographic transparency.

Therefore, future research endeavors should aim to investigate these phenomena cross-linguistically to uncover the generalizability of our findings and to delineate the specificities of how reading influences speech perception in diverse linguistic contexts.

Our study revealed that more proficient readers displayed greater sensitivity to AV cues, and that the relationship between reading proficiency and AV speech sensitivity in a phonologically transparent language was not significantly dependent on PA.

Future investigations should delve into diverse linguistic contexts, scrutinize age-related influences more comprehensively, and explore how the mediating role of PA on the relationship between reading proficiency and AV speech sensitivity might differ as a function of orthographic transparency in greater detail.

Such efforts will contribute significantly to our understanding of how these elements converge and, in turn, inform the development of tailored interventions for children facing challenges in reading and speech domains.

text.text: Mediation by PA:Learning to read helps develop stronger PA skills among readers.
These enhanced PA skills, in turn, may increase sensitivity to AV cues in speech perception.
In other words, as reading proficiency improves alongside enhanced PA, sensitivity to AV cues increases.

We predicted that PA would partially mediate the relationship between reading skills and sensitivity to AV cues in readers, with stronger PA skills associated with higher sensitivity to AV cues among proficient readers.Investigating how children process AV information alongside learning to read can inform the cognitive mechanisms underlying the increase in sensitivity to AV speech cues between 6 and 9 years reported in existing studies.

Exploring how reading and speech perception processes intersect in a transparent orthography can further increase our understanding how the regularity of visual representations in a writing system influences children's ability to recognize phonetic patterns in spoken language. 143 boys and 140 girls) aged 5 to 10 years (M=7.52, SD=1.84) participated in this study.
Participants were part of a larger study examining speech perception, language, and reading.

The younger pre-readers group, consisting of children aged 5-6 years, comprised 121 participants from a preschool (61 girls), while the older readers group, consisting of children aged 7-10 years (grades 1-4), included 200 participants (98 girls) from an elementary school in Tashkent, Uzbekistan.
It is important to note that in Uzbekistan, children are 7 years old when admitted to first grade and start formal reading instruction.
At the time of testing, 6-year-olds in our pre-readers group were younger than 6 years 9 months and thus had not yet started their formal reading instruction.
The pre-readers group completed PA and AV speech perception tasks, while the readers group completed the same PA and AV tasks, and additionally, completed a series of reading tasks (see Table1).
All participants were native speakers of Uzbek.
Among them, 159 children were proficient speakers and readers in Uzbek and Russian, while 162 were monolingual, proficient in Uzbek.
